fields.title: Just One More Scroll
fields.description:
Just One More Scroll
It usually starts innocently.
You get into bed at 11:30. You tell yourself you’ll sleep in five minutes. So naturally, you open Instagram.
One reel. Then another.
Then somehow, you are watching a 47-part story about a woman who quit her job, moved to Italy, and makes pottery for a living. You don’t even like pottery.
You check the time.
1:17 a.m.
You panic for approximately three seconds before deciding that, since you’ve already stayed up this late, you might as well keep scrolling.
And that’s how tomorrow’s tiredness is created.
We often think staying up late is just about losing a few hours of sleep. But it slowly starts affecting much more than the number of hours we spend in bed. Our mornings become harder, our attention gets worse, our patience becomes suspiciously low, and suddenly the smallest inconvenience feels like a personal attack.
The problem isn’t necessarily the phone itself. It’s the combination of endless scrolling and delayed sleep. There is always another video, another notification, another message, another piece of information waiting for us. There is no natural ending point. A book eventually has a last page. A television episode eventually ends. Instagram seems to have personally decided that you should never experience closure.
And the more tired we get, the harder it becomes to stop.
Research has consistently connected nighttime screen use with poorer sleep, particularly among children and adolescents. A National Sleep Foundation expert panel found that screen use and the content consumed before sleep can interfere with sleep health in children and teenagers.
There is also the obvious problem: you are choosing to stay awake.
If you scroll until 2 a.m. and have to wake up at 7, your body isn’t going to accept the explanation that “but I was watching something really interesting.”
Teenagers generally need around 8–10 hours of sleep, according to the CDC. Most of us know this. We just seem to treat sleep recommendations like terms and conditions, something we technically agree to but never actually read.
The effects show up the next day.
You wake up tired. You press snooze five times. You walk into class and spend the first ten minutes trying to remember why you’re there. You read the same sentence three times. You have work to finish, but your brain suddenly considers staring at the wall a perfectly reasonable alternative.
Sleep matters for concentration, mood, and how well we function during the day. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute even describes sleep as something people often sacrifice when life gets busy, despite the fact that enough sleep can support being happier and more productive during the day.
And then there is the mood.
When you’re exhausted, everything feels slightly more dramatic. A small disagreement becomes a huge argument. A bad grade feels like the end of your academic career. Someone leaving you on “seen” suddenly becomes a philosophical crisis.
Of course, one late night isn’t going to ruin your life. Sometimes you genuinely have an assignment, an exam, a late conversation, or simply a bad night. The problem is when “I’ll sleep early tomorrow” becomes a daily promise that tomorrow never seems to keep.
There is another interesting part of this habit: sometimes we don’t even scroll because we’re entertained. We scroll because we don’t want the day to end.
During the day, there are classes, work, expectations, conversations, and responsibilities. At night, nobody is asking anything from you. It’s quiet. Your phone becomes a tiny doorway into a world where you don’t have to think about tomorrow yet.
That can make staying awake feel like stealing time back for yourself.
But eventually, you’re not really getting extra time. You’re borrowing it from tomorrow.
And tomorrow collects the debt.
You don’t have to completely delete every social media app, throw your phone into a river, and become a monk. The solution can be much less dramatic. Putting the phone away a little earlier, turning off unnecessary notifications, having a consistent bedtime, or simply deciding that “one more reel” is actually the last reel can make a difference. The NIH recommends using the period before bed for quieter activities and limiting bright artificial light.
Maybe the real challenge is learning that not every quiet moment needs to be filled.
Sometimes you can just lie there. Think.
Because the next morning, your future self is going to have to deal with whatever your 1 a.m. self decided was more important than going to bed.
And honestly, your future self deserves better than that.
fields.author: Ishita

fields.title: A Little Comfort on a Bad Day
fields.description:
A Little Comfort on a Bad Day
There are some days when cooking feels like an unreasonable amount of effort.
You could make a salad. You could eat something healthy. You could prepare an actual meal with vegetables and protein and all the things you’re supposed to eat.
Instead, you are standing in front of the fridge at 9 p.m., emotionally exhausted, holding a tub of ice cream like it contains the answers to your problems.
And honestly, sometimes it helps.
There is something strangely comforting about food on a bad day. Maybe it’s a bowl of creamy mac and cheese, a grilled cheese sandwich with tomato soup, a plate of crispy fries, or a giant bowl of ramen that is probably much too hot, but you eat it anyway.
Comfort food is not really about being hungry.
Sometimes, it’s about wanting something familiar.
Food can be tied to memories, routines, and people. A particular soup might remind you of being sick as a child and having someone look after you. Pancakes on a Sunday morning might remind you of home. Chocolate chip cookies might remind you of baking with friends. Even something as simple as a bowl of warm pasta can feel reassuring when everything else feels slightly out of control.
And that’s probably why comfort food exists in almost every culture.
In the United States, it might be mac and cheese, mashed potatoes, grilled cheese, or chicken noodle soup. In Italy, a bowl of warm pasta can be the ultimate uncomplicated meal. In Japan, ramen and okayu, a soft rice porridge, are often associated with warmth and comfort. In France, there is something deeply reassuring about a bowl of onion soup or a warm gratin.
Different countries, different foods, same basic idea:
“Today was awful. Give me something warm.”
There is actually some science behind why certain foods can feel comforting. Food is connected to memory, emotion, and reward, and eating something we enjoy can activate the brain’s reward systems. But comfort food isn’t a magical cure for sadness. Eating a tub of ice cream will not solve your exam results, fix your friendship, or make tomorrow’s 8 a.m. class disappear.
Unfortunately.
What it can do is give you a small moment of pleasure when the rest of the day hasn’t been particularly generous.
And maybe that’s enough.
We sometimes talk about food as if every meal needs to be perfectly nutritious, perfectly balanced, and carefully planned. Of course, nutrition matters. But food is also social. It is cultural. It is emotional. We celebrate with it, connect over it, and sometimes use it to take care of ourselves.
The problem begins when food becomes the only way we know how to cope.
There is a difference between “I’m having a horrible day, so I’m making myself some hot chocolate” and “I’m having a horrible day, and eating is the only thing that makes me feel okay.”
The first can simply be comfort.
The second might be a sign that something else needs attention.
So maybe comfort food doesn’t need to be either glorified or villainised. It can just be what it is: a small form of comfort.
Sometimes that means making a bowl of tomato soup and grilled cheese when you don’t feel like talking. Sometimes it’s ordering pizza with your friends after a terrible week. Sometimes it’s eating cereal straight from the bowl while watching an old movie you’ve seen seventeen times.
And sometimes it’s sitting on the kitchen floor at midnight, eating leftover pasta because the day was terrible and you needed something that didn’t ask questions.
Not every bad day needs a life lesson.
Sometimes you just need something warm, something familiar, and a little time.
The next morning, the problem might still be there. The deadline might still exist. The awkward conversation might still need to happen.
But for tonight, at least, you had dinner. And maybe that is a pretty good place to start. :)
fields.author: Ishita

fields.title: You Don’t Have to Love Your Body Every Day
fields.description:
You Don’t Have to Love Your Body Every Day
There are days when you look in the mirror and think, “Wow. I look good.”
And then there are days when you look in the mirror, immediately change your outfit three times, and decide that mirrors are probably unnecessary inventions.
We’ve been told that the solution is body positivity. Love your body. Celebrate every part of it. Look in the mirror and remind yourself that you are beautiful.
It’s a nice idea. But what if you don’t feel beautiful that day?
What if you’re bloated? What if your skin is breaking out? What if your clothes don’t fit the way you wanted them to? What if you’re just having one of those days when you don’t particularly like what you see?
Trying to convince yourself that you love your body can sometimes feel like another thing you’re failing at.
This is where body neutrality comes in. Instead of asking you to love your body, body neutrality asks you to stop making your body responsible for your happiness.
Your body doesn’t have to be beautiful every day. It doesn’t have to be your favourite thing about yourself. It doesn’t even have to be something you think about that much.
Your body is simply… your body.
It gets you to class. It lets you hug your friends. It carries your groceries. It dances badly at parties. It gets tired. It gets sick. It changes. It grows. It sometimes makes weird noises at extremely inappropriate moments.
And perhaps that is enough.
The idea of body neutrality is partly about shifting the focus from how your body looks to what your body does and how you treat it. Instead of standing in front of a mirror trying to convince yourself that every part of you is beautiful, you might simply think, “This is my body today. I don’t need to judge it.”
That sounds much easier.
Because realistically, nobody is going to wake up every morning overflowing with unconditional love for their stomach, thighs, nose, hair, skin, and every other body part.
Some mornings you feel great. Some mornings you don’t. And neither feeling needs to become a verdict about your worth.
Social media makes this particularly difficult. We are constantly looking at carefully chosen photographs of people who appear to have perfect skin, perfect bodies, perfect hair, and somehow perfect lighting at all times. Meanwhile, we’re looking at ourselves under the fluorescent light in a bathroom that was clearly designed by someone who hates human beings.
It is very easy to start comparing. But body neutrality offers another way of thinking: maybe you don’t need to win the comparison. Maybe you can simply stop playing.
You can exercise because it makes you feel stronger, not because you need to punish yourself for eating dessert.
You can eat vegetables because they make you feel good, while also eating the pizza because, well, pizza.
You can wear clothes that make you comfortable instead of constantly asking whether they make you look thinner.
And you can have a bad body-image day without turning it into a bad-self-worth day.
There is also something freeing about accepting that your body will change.
Weight changes. Skin changes. Hair changes. Bodies age. Hormones do their own mysterious little experiments. You cannot realistically spend your entire life trying to keep your body exactly the same.
So maybe the goal isn’t to love every version of yourself.
Maybe it’s to make peace with the fact that there will be many versions of yourself.
Body positivity says, “I love my body.”
Body neutrality says, “My body is not the most interesting thing about me.”
And honestly, that can be a relief. Because you have other things to worry about.
Your friendships. Your work. Your ambitions. The book you’re reading. The person you have a crush on. Why you opened your phone five minutes ago and have already forgotten what you were supposed to do.
Your body can simply exist in the background while you get on with your life. You don’t have to love your reflection every day.
You just have to remember that you are more than a reflection.
By Ishita
fields.author: Ishita

fields.title: What if they find out?
fields.description:
What if they find out?
The strange feeling of not believing you deserve the things you worked for.
You made it.
You got the grade you had been studying for for what felt like forever.
Everyone is proud of you. Your parents, your teachers, even your fellow students who were studying alongside you. They all think you did a good job.
And you did.
You studied hard. You worked for it. You reached the goal you had set for yourself.
So why is the only thought you can seem to hold onto:
“It was just luck.”
Maybe the exam was easy.
Maybe the teacher was generous.
Maybe everyone else simply did worse.
You push the thought away.
A few weeks later, the same thing happens again.
Someone compliments your art.
You laugh it off.
“It’s not that good.”
or
“Everyone else did way better.”
A month later, you get accepted into the university you desperately wanted to go to.
You stare at the email.
You should be thinking:
“I did it!”
Instead:
“Was the competition weaker this year?”
And there it is again.
That uncomfortable little voice telling you that somehow, somewhere along the way, you convinced everyone that you're more capable than you really are.
The fear that eventually, someone will notice.
That they'll look at you and think:
“Wait. You're not actually supposed to be here.”
That feeling has a name.
Imposter syndrome.

But I actually did it.
That's the weird thing about imposter syndrome.
You’re not necessarily bad at something. Mostly, it's almost the opposite.
You can have the grades, the awards, the compliments, the opportunities. You can have years of evidence that you're capable.
And still feel like you're pretending.
Your brain finds a reason for every success.
Good grade? Easy test.
Getting selected? Nobody else applied.
Someone complimented you? They're just being nice.
Success? Luck.
And somehow, your failures determine who you really are.
One bad grade? That’s just who I am.
One awkward presentation? Everyone can tell I'm terrible at this.
One mistake? I knew I didn't belong here.
Your successes become exceptions.
Your failures become evidence.
And before you know it, you've created a version of reality where almost nothing you do can convince you that you're actually good enough.

The finish line keeps moving
Maybe you think you'll finally feel confident once you achieve the thing.
Once you get the grade.
Once you win the competition.
Once someone finally tells you that you're good enough.
And then you get there.
But the finish line moves.
Right when you're about to reach it.
An A becomes an A+.
Being good becomes being the best.
Doing well becomes never struggling.
Eventually, you're not even chasing success anymore.
You're chasing the feeling that you're allowed to have succeeded.
The problem is that feeling never seems to arrive.
There's always another thing you could have done better. Someone you could be more like. Something you could achieve next.
So you keep going.
Not because you want to anymore, but because you're scared that if you stop, someone might finally notice you're not as capable as they thought.

Then you look around
And this is where it gets unfair.
Everyone else seems so sure of themselves.
You see someone get an A after saying they barely studied.
Your friend got the internship that rejected you.
You open Instagram and see someone your age winning competitions, travelling, creating things, pushing forward.
And suddenly you're wondering:
“What am I even doing?”
But there's something we forget when we compare ourselves to other people.
You're seeing the finished version.
You don't see their mistakes.
You don't see the things they don't understand.
You don't see the nights they felt completely lost.
You don't see them questioning themselves.
You only see what they decided to show you.
But here's what you don't see.
You're not the only one struggling with imposter syndrome.
It's actually quite common.
Many teens, and even adults, experience it.
When getting into university.
When joining a new work environment.
When stepping into any room where everyone else seems to know what they're doing.
You're not alone with that feeling.
And the strange thing is, it tends to hit the people who care the most.
The ones who take their work seriously.
Who want to get it right.
Who actually belong.
Because if you didn't care, you wouldn't be worrying whether you're good enough in the first place.

So… am I actually an imposter?
Probably not.
Feeling like an imposter doesn't mean you are one.
You don't have to know everything to deserve your place somewhere.
You don't have to be the smartest person in the room.
You don't even have to feel confident.
Sometimes you'll be the person who knows the least.
Sometimes you'll ask the question everyone else seemed to already know the answer to.
Sometimes you'll mess something up.
None of that means you tricked anyone.
It means you're learning.
And learning is supposed to feel uncomfortable sometimes.
Sometimes belonging looks like sitting in a room thinking,
“I have absolutely no idea what I'm doing.”
…and staying anyway.

Maybe we're asking the wrong question
We spend so much time asking:
“Am I good enough?”
But that's a horrible question to live by.
Because there will always be someone better. Another achievement. Another grade. Another person to compare yourself to.
So maybe you're allowed to still be learning.
To be nervous.
To not know.
To get things wrong.
Maybe you're even allowed to be proud of yourself without explaining to yourself why it doesn't count.
And maybe
just maybe
you didn't fool anyone.
Maybe the achievement wasn't a fluke.
Maybe you actually did earn your place.
And maybe the problem was never that you weren't good enough.
Maybe you just haven't learned how to believe it yet.
fields.author: Johanna Huber

fields.title: A Cozy Mental-Reset
fields.description:
Title: A Cozy Mental-Reset

No matter the season, making space for a cozy night or even a whole weekend can be a lovely way to slow down, recharge, and give your mind a little breathing room. So, for my fellow lazy planners, I’ve curated a little “menu” of low-effort options for a mental refresh, all from the comfort of your own room, with a few scented candles, maybe!

Think of it as a choose-your-own-reset. Pick whatever sounds good, skip whatever doesn’t, and make the evening your own.Snack Options (with links to recipes):
🍓Snack Options 
What’s a cozy night without snacks? Here are a few easy options, from sweet to salty:
Healthy overnight oats drizzled with honey and berries (+ low-effort, inexpensive)
https://www.31daily.com/overnight-oats-with-blueberries/#recipe
Sweet Potato Chips Fried/Baked with Avocado Oil (good alternative to processed chips)
https://saladinajar.com/recipes/vegetables-and-side-dishes/skinny-sweet-potato-chips/#recipe
https://www.julieseatsandtreats.com/air-fryer-sweet-potato-chips/
Granola Chocolate + Almond/Peanut Butter Barks
https://lovelydelites.com/no-bake-peanut-butter-chocolate-granola-bark/#recipe
Homemade Popcorn Drizzled in Olive Oil + Sprinkled with Sea Salt
https://www.oatmealwithafork.com/olive-oil-popcorn/#recipe
Fruit Sorbet (needs a food processor, can be watermelon, mango, strawberry, and more!)
https://www.elizabethrider.com/sorbet-recipe/#tasty-recipes-16178-jump-target

Pick Your Entertainment 🎬
Now for the most important part: choosing what to watch. To save you from spending 45 minutes scrolling through streaming services, here’s a little menu for every mood.
🌸 Animation
Kiki’s Delivery Service
My Neighbor Totoro
Whisper of the Heart
Inside Out
Ponyo
☕ Comedy & Comfort
Gilmore Girls | series
Never Have I Ever | series
Brooklyn Nine-Nine | series
The Princess Diaries
The Grand Budapest Hotel
🕵️ Thriller
Rear Window
Catch Me If You Can
Now You See Me
Inception
Ocean’s Eleven
💌 Romance
The Love Hypothesis
Pride & Prejudice (2005)
How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
Bridget Jones’s Diary
Legally Blonde
🦇 Spooky
Coraline
Beetlejuice
Stranger Things | series
Scary Movie (2000)
This Is the End (2013)
🔎 Mystery
A Series of Unfortunate Events | series
Knives Out
Only Murders in the Building | series
Enola Holmes
Wednesday | series

Your Reset, Your Rules
There’s no perfect formula for a mental reset. Maybe yours involves popcorn, ice cream, and three episodes of Gilmore Girls. Or maybe it’s reading a classic novel or lying in bed and listening to music.
Remember that you don’t have to make your reset productive. Life is stressful and chaotic enough. Give yourself some rest, put your to-do list aside for a little while, and let yourself simply be.
Sometimes, the coziest thing you can do is give yourself permission to do nothing at all. ♡
By Ruby and Sophia
fields.author: Ruby and Sophia

fields.title: YOU WERE MY MEANING
fields.description:
YOU WERE MY MEANING

I wanted to live loudly,
dance in the rain,
feel the sun on my skin,
let the wind run through my hair.

Then you came along.

Late-night conversations.
Laughing until we couldn’t breathe.
Those quiet moments
when a look said everything.

Somehow,
I mistook you for home.

I made you my light
until I forgot
I could shine on my own.

And when you left,
I thought I had lost everything.

But maybe
I had only lost
the version of me
that existed around you.

And maybe
finding myself again
is the meaning
I was looking for all along.

By Sophia
fields.author: Sophia

fields.title: Echo der Gedanken
fields.description:
Echo der Gedanken
Tränen laufen mein Gesicht herunter,
hab’ das Gefühl ich werd’ nicht mehr Munter.
Die Gedanken werden laut,
ein warmes Gefühl auf meiner Haut.
Bin so müde, doch krieg kein Auge zu,
schließlich lässt mein Kopf mir keine Ruh.
So viele Gedanken schwirren umher,
fluten meinen Kopf so wie das Meer.
Mein Handy leuchtet neben mir,
auf dem Bildschirm steht: Wir haben’s schon halb vier.
Um 1 da fing ich an,
mit der Suche nach einer Therapie denn ich bang.
Um mich selbst und mein Leben,
will ja eigentlich nach viel mehr noch streben.
Denn sind die Wartezeiten nicht lang genug,
sorgt die Gesellschaft für weiteren Verzug.
Drum warten und warten die jungen Menschen,
bis sie ab Januar 2027 vielleicht noch mehr um Plätze kämpfen.
„Budgetierung“ ist hier das Wort,
welches schon bald für Aufstand sorgt.
Spätestens wenn die Mutter berichtet,
dass diese hat ihren Sohn vernichtet.
Drum bettelte er um Hilfe,
doch die Warteliste war so lang,
da kam er bis an Lebensende nicht dran.
Und sind die Plätze noch so wichtig,
wird die Jugend dem Land ja nicht pflichtig.
Immer ist sie der Politik zu viel,
bis man sie braucht, aber bitte stabil.
Dank der Budgetierung, oh nein,
könnte der Zugang zu Therapie bald schwieriger sein.
Rund 500 junge Menschen jedes Jahr
sterben durch Suizid und das ist wirklich wahr.
Eine der häufigsten Todesursachen bei den jungen Menschen,
doch trotzdem lässt man sie immer mehr alleine kämpfen.
Immer wieder wird weggeguckt,
alles mit den Schultern bloß „weggezuckt“.
Keine Minute wird an die sterbenden Jugendlichen verschwendet,
lieber für wichtigere Dinge verwendet.
Ich ersticke. Spüre wie mein Hals verengt,
der Lebenswille wird einfach verdrängt.
Meine dritte Absage in 10 Minuten,
ich fange immer mehr an zu bluten.
Die Gedanken rasen,
über meinem Kopf schweben Blasen.
Blasen der ewigen Gedanken,
die auch mich immer mehr zanken.
Wir sind echt –
und jetzt erst recht.
Hört uns zu,
bitte gebt keine Ruh.
Kämpft für die Gerechtigkeit,
denn dafür ist’s schon lange Zeit.
Lasst die Lebenswillen stärken,
lasst die Jugendlichen Liebe merken.
By Sanja
fields.author: Sanja

fields.title: Shards
fields.description:
Shards
Content note: bipolar disorder, hearing voices, suicidal thoughts
Every morning Alice puts a glass of water in front of me and lays a tablet beside it.
“I have to run,” she says, her rucksack already over one shoulder. “Seminar until four. Then I’m baking. Be excited.”
“I’m trembling with joy.”
She grins, her eyes flick towards the glass and back again.
Alice stayed when everyone else turned away after my bipolar diagnosis, and she decided to trust me. For her, it is that simple.
The door clicks shut.
I wait till I can no longer hear her footsteps on the stairs.
Then I carry the tablet to the bathroom and flush it away.
It’s been going on for weeks.
On the antipsychotics, everything is muffled. I’m not sad, I’m not happy, I’m simply present.
Without them, the voices come back in.
But at least then I’m not alone.
That is what I tell myself, anyway.
I don’t have much to do during the day. In the middle of my final exams, I fell into a severe depression. My therapist would say I nosedived from euthymia straight into a depressive episode. I would say my brain pulled the emergency brake and threw me out of the carriage.
Even the worst university in London turned me down afterwards, and that one is notorious for employing corrupt professors.
My part-time job at the clothes shop went too. “Increasing aggression,” they called it.
You mere mortals can picture my life as a roller coaster.
For two minutes, it has its thrill. For a whole lifetime, it most certainly does not.
So I sit in front of the television.
“KALI, KALI, KALI!”
The American Ballet Theatre erupts as she steps onto the stage. On the sofa in our flat, I clap until my fingers sting.
She dances as if in a trance. Ballet and Bharatanatyam in a single body, all colour and precision.
Everyone knows her story by now. The daughter of a Devadasi who became one of the most respected dancers in the world. Her life was anything but easy. Still, there is happiness in her eyes.
The kind I want so badly for myself.
As long as she dances, it is quiet in my head.
There you go, I think.
It works without tablets. All I need is a dancer on repeat.
Shortly after four, the key turns in the lock.
“Marlee?”
Alice stands in the doorway with that anxious look on her face.
It can only mean one thing.
“Your mother called. She called me because you don’t pick up.”
“And?”
She doesn’t meet my eyes. She shifts her weight from one foot to the other.
“Why don’t you pick up? People can change, you know.”
I sigh.
She really has to stop seeing the good in everyone. Sooner or later, she will be disappointed, and when that day comes, I don’t want to be there to watch her break.
One broken person per flat is enough.
Besides, I know what my mother would say.
What a colossal disappointment I am.
The day has been good so far. I’m certainly not going to let a bitter woman in the middle of a midlife crisis ruin it.
“The last time I trusted her, I ended up on a psychiatric ward,” I say. “And believe me, even someone as disgustingly cheerful as you would come out of one visit depressed.”
Alice raises an eyebrow.
“Well. Good thing the two of us can trust each other, then.”
The water glass from this morning is still on the table.
It is empty.
“Yes,” I say quietly. “Of course.”
I don’t tell her.
I of all people know how far she would go to keep the only person she has left. She would call my mother. She would call the hospital.
And afterwards, she would never look at me the way she does now.
Around seven, something smells burnt.
I look towards the kitchen.
What on earth has she done this time?
“NO! My Quarkbällchen!”
This would not have happened if she had simply let me buy them, the way the rest of society does. But no. Ever since she found her German grandmother’s recipe, apparently we have been required to demonstrate our complete lack of baking talent and destroy Marlee’s stomach.
She comes running in with a bowl, holding black, misshapen creatures under my nose.
Whatever these are, they’re certainly not Quarkbällchen.
“Try one,” she says brightly. “A little burnt, but they turned out really well. Never judge a Quarkbällchen by its cover. That’s all I’m saying.”
She perches on the arm of the sofa, flour on her cheek, beaming at me.
She baked for me after eight hours at university.
She put the glass in front of me this morning.
And a little while ago, for the first time today, someone whispered inside my head.
Alice, I have to tell you something.
The sentence is sitting ready on my tongue.
“Alice,” I say, “you cannot possibly eat those carcinogenic things.”
She looks at me as if I’ve grown horns.
“Carcinogenic? Why would Quarkbällchen be carcinogenic? Unhealthy because of all the sugar, fine, I’m aware of that, but otherwise?”
I cannot for the life of me believe that this person studies at one of the most prestigious universities in England.
She eats three.
I say nothing more.
At night, I lie awake.
Alice is asleep next door. A rerun of Kali’s performance is playing on the television, the sound turned off. I know the music by heart anyway.
At noon, it worked.
Now it doesn’t.
The voices are louder than the music in my head.
Murderer.
Disappointment.
The second one sounds suspiciously like my mother.
It is as if my soul were made of shards.
Depending on the angle, depending on which piece you look at, the colour changes.
At noon they were red and white: love and innocence.
Now the same colours mean something else.
Blood.
Naivety.
Guilt without a clear reason.
The horrible feeling that everything would be easier if I stopped being a problem.
I have thought it before.
What frightens me tonight is how reasonable it sounds.
I watch Kali turn.
I once saw an interview with her. Someone asked how she had made it, and she said she hadn’t made it on her own.
Back then, I found the answer disappointing.
I get up.
Alice’s door is ajar. She sleeps with her mouth open, one arm hanging out of the bed. On her bedside table sits the bowl of Quarkbällchen.
It is empty.
Of course.
“Alice.”
She jolts upright.
“What? Is something burning?”
“Not this time.”
She rubs her eyes. Then she looks at me, and the sleep drains from her face.
“Marlee. What’s wrong?”
I had sentences prepared.
They are all gone.
“I’m not taking them,” I say.
She waits.
“The tablets. Not for weeks. I flush them away as soon as you’re out of the door.”
Silence.
“The voices are back.” My mouth is dry. “And tonight I’m thinking things that scare me.”
There it is.
The moment I’ve been trying not to imagine.
The phone call to my mother.
The hospital.
That look.
Instead, Alice throws back the duvet and shuffles towards the wall.
“Come here.”
I lie down beside her.
She smells of burnt sugar.
“Are you angry?” I ask.
“Furious.”
Her voice is shaking.
“And glad you woke me. Both at once.”
For a while, neither of us says anything.
“Tomorrow morning, we call your therapist,” she says eventually. “You talk. I sit next to you.”
I stare at the ceiling.
“And if she says you need to go to hospital,” Alice continues, “I’m coming with you.”
I turn my head towards her.
“And I’m bringing Quarkbällchen.”
“You’ll poison the entire ward.”
“At least it will keep everyone busy.”
I laugh.
“And the glass,” she says.
“What about it?”
“From tomorrow, I’m standing right there until it’s empty.”
“You’ll be late for your seminar.”
“Then I’ll be late.”
The phone in my hand vibrates.
Mum.
Half past two in the morning.
She probably can’t sleep either.
I don’t answer.
I put the phone on the duvet and let it buzz until it stops by itself.
The voices are still there.
So is Alice’s breathing beside me.
The night hasn’t become easier.
Five more hours until morning.
But this time, I don’t have to get through them alone.
By Sophia
fields.author: Sophia

fields.title: Der lange Weg zur Heilung
fields.description:
Hinweis zu sensiblen Inhalten: Diese Geschichte enthält Bezüge zum Tod eines Kindes, politischer Verfolgung, Inhaftierung, Trauer, Trauma und Panikattacken.
Der lange Weg zur Heilung
„Pazilya, steh auf! Schon spät, Süße. Auch heute keine neue Regel für dich, Schule wichtig!“
Träge drehe ich mich um. Das Gesicht meiner Mutter wird weicher, als sich unsere Blicke treffen. Mir steigen jedoch urplötzlich Tränen in die Augen, als ich wahrnehme, wie ihr einst so hübsches Gesicht nun von Falten durchfurcht ist. Es ist verrückt, wie schnell diese verkorkste Welt sie hat altern lassen. Ihre dunklen Augen, die früher wie Bernstein leuchteten, sind matt geworden. Die Hände, die uns als Kinder sanft durch die Haare strichen, zittern jetzt manchmal beim Teekochen.
Ich weiß, meine Mutter möchte, dass ich weitermache, mein Leben lebe, so wie auch sie versucht, für mich weiterzumachen. Doch ich möchte nicht raus, nur den Tag an mir vorbeiziehen lassen. Ich bin siebzehn, aber fühle mich wie siebzig. Meine langen schwarzen Haare hängen ungekämmt um mein schmales Gesicht, meine Haut ist fahl geworden, seit wir in Deutschland sind. Ich sehe aus wie ein Geist, ein perfektes Spiegelbild dessen, was in mir vorgeht.
Ich konnte nicht schlafen, musste immerzu daran denken: ihr Schreien, als sie von uns weggenommen worden war. Mamas Flehen, sie sollen sie doch bitte nicht ins staatliche Internat schicken. Wir wussten alle, was es bedeutete.
Also tat ich das Einzige, was mir sinnvoll erschien, was meine Pflicht war. Ich beschützte meine kleine Schwester Dilnur, bot mich an ihrer Stelle an.
Natürlich wollten sie mich nicht. Ich war zu alt für das Internat und wurde in der Fabrik gebraucht. Sonst, sagten sie, hätten sie natürlich uns beide mitgenommen.
Dilnur war erst zwölf Jahre alt, mit diesen ungewöhnlichen violett-blauen Augen, die in unserer Familie einzigartig waren. Wir waren immer neidisch auf ihre besondere Augenfarbe und haben gesagt, in ganz Xinjiang gäbe es kein schöneres Mädchen als sie. Mit ihrem ansteckenden Lachen, das wie Windspiele klang, und ihrer bedingungslosen Liebe.
Manchmal hasse ich sie dafür. Dafür, dass sie mich allein gelassen hat. Dafür, dass sie aufgegeben hat. Und dann hasse ich mich dafür, dass ich sie hasse. Es ist ein Kreislauf, aus dem ich nicht herauskomme.
Monate später erhaschten wir einen kurzen Blick auf sie, als sie zwischen zwei Gebäuden hindurchgeführt wurde. Es war genug, um ihre glasigen Augen zu sehen, die bereits in diesem jungen Alter zu viel erlebt hatten, sowie ihre gräulichen, eingefallenen Wangen. Sie war nur noch ein Geist von sich selbst.
Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wussten wir noch nicht, dass dies das letzte Mal sein würde, dass wir sie sehen.
Einige Zeit später erreichte uns die Nachricht. Sie wäre tot. Man sagte uns, sie habe sich das Leben genommen.
Ihre Leiche bekamen wir nie. Der Transport wäre zu viel Arbeit gewesen, meinten sie. Sie ließen meine Schwester irgendwo zurück, als wäre sie nichts als ein Körper, um den sich niemand mehr kümmern musste.
Nach ihrem Tod flohen meine Mutter und ich hierher. So sehr wir unsere Heimat auch liebten, China liebte uns gewiss nicht zurück.
Hier in Deutschland sollte alles besser werden. Das haben sie uns zumindest versprochen. Die meisten erfuhren erst bei den Olympischen Winterspielen in Peking von unserer Lage, und plötzlich gab es überall Solidaritätsbekundungen. Aber danach kam nichts. Das Interesse verflog so schnell, wie es gekommen war.
In der Schule konnte ich keine Freundschaften schließen. Während alle über die neuesten TikTok-Trends diskutieren, darüber, wer mit wem zusammen ist oder welche Handtaschen gerade angesagt sind, sitze ich still da. Denke an meine kleine Schwester. An die Lager. An alle, die noch dort sind.
Letzte Woche hat Frau Müller, unsere Geschichtslehrerin, über den Holocaust gesprochen und gesagt: „So etwas darf nie wieder passieren.“
Ich habe mich gemeldet und gesagt: „Aber es passiert doch gerade. In China. Mit den Uiguren.“
Sie hat mich angesehen, als hätte ich etwas Unanständiges gesagt.
„Das ist ein komplexes geopolitisches Thema, Pazilya. Nicht vergleichbar.“
Danach haben mich ein paar aus meiner Klasse angestarrt, als wäre ich verrückt. Seitdem melde ich mich nicht mehr.
Und jetzt, an ihrem Todestag, soll ich lächelnd rumlaufen? So tun, als wäre alles in Ordnung? In der Schule aufpassen, als wäre heute ein Tag wie jeder andere?
Ich glaube nicht, dass ich das schaffe.
Es ist, als wäre mit ihrem Tod auch ein Teil von mir selbst gestorben.
Doch ich weiß, was meine Mutter von mir erwartet. Ich bin alles, was ihr noch geblieben ist.
Wieder sagt sie: „Geh, zieh dich um.“
Also gehe ich. Ich höre auf sie. Ich möchte nicht auch noch meine Mutter im Stich lassen.
Auf dem Weg zur Schule sehe ich etwas im Gras glitzern. Eine Haarspange. Eine Stoffblume ist daran befestigt, wahrscheinlich eine Hyazinthe. Der Clip ist verbogen, ein Blütenblatt hängt nur noch an einem Faden.
Wahrscheinlich hat ein Kind sie verloren.
Die Spange ist violett. Wie Dilnurs Augen. Wie die Blumen, die sie immer in unser Haar geflochten hat, wenn wir im Sommer in Xinjiang auf den Wiesen lagen und uns die Geschichten ausgedacht haben, die wir eines Tages schreiben würden.
Ich hebe mein Fundstück auf. Weiß nicht warum. Ist ja nicht so, als könnte ich sie zurückgeben.
Aber ich stecke sie ein.
Dann, nach einem Moment, klemme ich sie mir doch hinter das Ohr.
Fast wäre ich auf einen Regenwurm getreten. Ich weiche im letzten Moment aus und muss unwillkürlich lächeln.
Dilnur hätte mir eine Predigt gehalten.
„Sie haben auch eine Familie! Wie würdest du dich fühlen, wenn du plötzlich stirbst?“
So eine kleine Person, die die Hände in die Hüften stemmt und dabei völlig ernst schaut. Mama und ich mussten immer lachen, was sie nur noch wütender machte.
Damals wussten wir noch nicht, dass sie uns eines Tages wirklich zeigen würde, wie es sich anfühlt.
Der Schmerz in meiner Brust kommt so plötzlich, dass ich stehen bleibe. Ich kann nicht atmen.
Was hat meine Therapeutin gesagt?
Einatmen bis vier, halten bis sieben, ausatmen bis acht.
Es funktioniert nicht. Ich zähle falsch, verliere den Rhythmus, kriege Panik, weil ich Panik habe.
Aber dann versuche ich es langsamer.
Es wird besser.
Meine Hände zittern noch.
„Hey?“
Ich zucke zusammen.
Ein Mädchen steht hinter mir, ungefähr so alt wie ich. Ihre lockigen Haare sind kunstvoll geflochten. Sie sieht besorgt aus.
„Alles okay?“
Ich nicke automatisch. Fasse mir an die Haarspange.
Bin plötzlich peinlich berührt.
Wie sehe ich wohl aus? Wie ein Flower-Power-Hippie aus San Francisco, der gerade einen Zusammenbruch auf offener Straße hatte. Fehlt nur noch, dass ich anfange, diesen alten Song von Scott McKenzie zu summen.
„Du bist doch die Neue aus der Schule, oder?“
Sie lächelt vorsichtig, aber es wirkt angestrengt.
„Ich bin Amy.“
„Pazilya.“
„Ich weiß.“
Sie zögert, tritt von einem Fuß auf den anderen.
„Ich habe gehört, was mit deiner Schwester passiert ist. Es tut mir wirklich leid.“
Mein ganzer Körper spannt sich an.
Wie toll. Die ganze Schule redet über mich.
„Was genau hast du gehört?“
Sie wird rot.
„Nur, dass sie weggebracht wurde. In China. Und dass sie …“
Sie stoppt abrupt und beißt sich auf die Lippe.
Ich sage nichts.
Was soll ich auch sagen?
„Es ist so schrecklich“, sagt Amy. Ihre Worte überschlagen sich fast. „Was dort passiert. Ich verstehe nicht, wie die Welt einfach zusehen kann.“
Sie atmet tief durch.
„Sorry. Ich rede zu viel. Meine Mama sagt immer, ich soll erst nachdenken, bevor ich rede, aber …“
Sie verstummt und schüttelt den Kopf über sich selbst.
Ich mustere sie.
Die meisten wissen kaum, wer wir Uiguren sind. Und hier steht ein fremdes Mädchen, das offensichtlich nicht weiß, was es sagen soll, aber es trotzdem versucht.
„Meine Eltern sind aus dem Kongo geflohen“, sagt Amy leise. „Vor dem Krieg. Aber auch hier haben wir Probleme. Mein Bruder wurde letzten Monat von drei Typen zusammengeschlagen. An der U-Bahn-Station.“
Sie lacht kurz auf, aber es klingt falsch.
„Gebrochene Nase. Er macht Witze darüber, sagt, er sieht jetzt aus wie ein Boxer. Aber nachts höre ich ihn manchmal weinen.“
„Das tut mir leid“, sage ich.
Sie zuckt mit den Schultern.
„Meine Eltern sagen ständig, dass die Geschichte sich wiederholt, aber keiner will es sehen.“
Zum ersten Mal seit Monaten fühle ich so etwas wie Verbindung.
„Ich bin in so einer Gruppe.“
Amy spielt nervös mit den Riemen ihres Rucksacks.
„Gegen Rechtsextremismus. Wir organisieren Demos und so. Samstag ist wieder eine auf dem Marktplatz.“
Sie zögert.
„Ehrlich gesagt fühlt es sich meistens sinnlos an. Wir stehen da mit unseren Schildern, dann gehen alle nach Hause und es ist, als wäre nichts gewesen. Aber ich weiß auch nicht, was ich sonst tun soll.“
Ich nicke. Weiß nicht, was ich sagen soll.
„Letztes Mal gab es Gegenproteste. Irgendwelche Typen haben uns angeschrien.“
Sie lacht wieder. Es klingt seltsam, unecht.
„Meine Freundinnen wollen nicht mehr mitkommen. Sie finden es zu gefährlich. Kann ich ihnen nicht mal verübeln.“
Sie sieht mich an und lächelt müde.
Ich denke an meine Schwester. An die Menschen in den Lagern und Gefängnissen. An Amys Bruder, der nachts weint. An uns beide. An meine Mutter.
Der Schmerz in meiner Brust kommt wieder, kurz und pochend.
Ich fasse mir unwillkürlich hinter das Ohr und spüre den verbogenen Clip der Haarspange. Er drückt unangenehm in die Haut.
„Wir könnten uns mal treffen.“
Amys Stimme wird leise.
„Am Sonntag? Wir könnten vielleicht in ein Café gehen, wenn du möchtest.“
Mein erster Impuls ist wegzulaufen.
Aber ich höre mich sagen:
„Vielleicht.“
Amy blinzelt überrascht.
„Echt jetzt?“
„Ich weiß nicht.“ Mein Herz hämmert. „Ich habe mich schon lange nicht mehr mit jemandem getroffen.“
„Dann kommst du vielleicht nicht.“
Amy kritzelt ihre Nummer auf einen zerknitterten Kassenbon. Ihre Handschrift ist kaum lesbar, zittrig.
„Ich warte trotzdem. Falls du es doch schaffst.“
Sie drückt mir den Zettel in die Hand. Ihre Handfläche ist verschwitzt.
„Dann vielleicht bis Sonntag.“
Ich nicke nur. Kann nichts mehr sagen.
Amy geht schon, dreht sich noch einmal um und hebt vorsichtig die Hand.
Dann ist sie weg.
Ich atme tief ein und gehe weiter zur Schule. Der Zettel ist zerknüllt in meiner Faust. Als ich das Klassenzimmer betrete, stecke ich ihn in meine Hosentasche.
Die erste Stunde ist Mathe.
Ich habe die Hausaufgaben nicht gemacht.
Draußen beginnt es zu nieseln. Einzelne Tropfen laufen die Fensterscheibe hinunter. Ich sehe mein Spiegelbild darin.
Die Haarspange ist kaum zu erkennen im trüben Licht.
Sie hält.
Aber wie lange, weiß ich nicht.

Diese Geschichte ist Fiktion. Alle Figuren sind erfunden. Der Hintergrund beruht auf dokumentierten Berichten, unter anderem auf dem Bericht des UN-Hochkommissariats für Menschenrechte zur Lage in Xinjiang aus dem Jahr 2022.
fields.author: Sophia Kanesarasa

fields.title: The Long Road to Healing
fields.description:
Content warning: This story contains references to the death of a child, political persecution, detention, grief, trauma, and panic attacks.
The Long Road to Healing
“Pazilya, get up! You’re already late, sweetheart. No new rule for you today either, school important!”
Reluctantly, I turn over. My mother’s face softens when our eyes meet. But tears rush to my eyes when I notice how her once beautiful face is now furrowed with wrinkles. It is insane how quickly this messed-up world has aged her. Her dark eyes, which used to glow like amber, have gone dull. The hands that gently stroked our hair when we were children now sometimes tremble when she makes tea.
I know my mother wants me to keep going, to live my life, just as she tries to keep going for me. But I don’t want to go out. I just want to let the day pass me by. I am seventeen, but I feel seventy. My long black hair hangs uncombed around my narrow face, and my skin has turned sallow since we came to Germany. I look like a ghost, a perfect reflection of what is going on inside me.
I couldn’t sleep. I kept thinking about it. Her screaming when she was taken from us. Mama begging them not to send her to the state boarding school. We all knew what it meant.
So I did the only thing that made sense to me, the thing that was my duty. I shielded my little sister Dilnur and offered myself in her place.
Of course they didn’t want me. I was too old for the boarding school and needed in the factory. Otherwise, they said, they would of course have taken us both.
Dilnur was only twelve, with those unusual violet-blue eyes that no one else in our family had. We were always jealous of that color and used to say there was no prettier girl in all of Xinjiang. With her contagious laugh that sounded like wind chimes, and her unconditional love.
Sometimes I hate her for it. For leaving me alone. For giving up. And then I hate myself for hating her. It is a cycle I can’t get out of.
Months later, we caught a brief glimpse of her as she was led between two buildings. It was enough to see her glassy eyes, which had already seen too much at such a young age, and her grayish, sunken cheeks. She was only a ghost of herself.
At that point, we did not yet know it would be the last time we saw her.
Some time later, the news reached us. She was dead. They told us she had taken her own life.
We never got her body. Transporting it would have been too much work, they said. They left my sister somewhere, as though she were nothing more than a body no one had to care for anymore.
After her death, my mother and I fled here. As much as we loved our homeland, China certainly did not love us back.
Here in Germany, everything was supposed to get better. At least, that’s what they promised us. Most people only learned about our situation during the Winter Olympics in Beijing, and suddenly there were declarations of solidarity everywhere. But after that, nothing. The interest faded as quickly as it had come.
I couldn’t make friends at school. While everyone discusses the latest TikTok trends, who is dating whom, or which handbags are in right now, I sit there in silence. Thinking about my little sister. About the camps. About everyone who is still there.
Last week, Frau Müller, our history teacher, talked about the Holocaust and said, “Something like that must never happen again.”
I raised my hand and said, “But it is happening right now. In China. To the Uyghurs.”
She looked at me as if I had said something indecent.
“That is a complex geopolitical issue, Pazilya. It’s not comparable.”
Afterwards, a few people in my class stared at me as if I were crazy. I haven’t raised my hand since.
And now, on the anniversary of her death, I’m supposed to walk around smiling? Act as if everything were fine? Pay attention in class as if today were a day like any other?
I don’t think I can do it.
It is as if a part of me died with her.
But I know what my mother expects of me. I am all she has left.
Again she says, “Go, get dressed.”
So I go. I listen to her. I don’t want to let my mother down, too.
On the way to school, I see something glinting in the grass. A hair clip. There’s a fabric flower on it, probably a hyacinth. The clip is bent, and one petal is hanging by a single thread.
A child probably lost it.
The clip is violet. Like Dilnur’s eyes. Like the flowers she always braided into our hair when we lay in the meadows in Xinjiang in summer, making up the stories we would write one day.
I pick up my find. I don’t know why. It’s not as if I could give it back.
But I put it in my pocket.
Then, after a moment, I clip it behind my ear after all.
I almost step on an earthworm. I swerve at the last second and can’t help smiling.
Dilnur would have given me a lecture.
“They have families too! How would you feel if you suddenly died?”
Such a tiny person, hands on her hips and completely serious. Mama and I always had to laugh, which only made her angrier.
Back then, we didn’t know she would one day show us what it actually felt like.
The pain in my chest comes so suddenly that I stop. I can’t breathe.
What did my therapist say?
Breathe in for four, hold for seven, breathe out for eight.
It doesn’t work. I miscount, lose the rhythm, panic because I’m panicking.
But then I try it more slowly.
It gets better.
My hands are still shaking.
“Hey?”
I flinch.
A girl is standing behind me, about my age. Her curly hair is intricately braided. She looks worried.
“Everything okay?”
I nod automatically. Touch the hair clip.
Suddenly I’m embarrassed.
What must I look like? Like a flower-power hippie from San Francisco who has just had a breakdown in the middle of the street. All that’s missing is me starting to hum that old Scott McKenzie song.
“You’re the new girl from school, right?”
She smiles cautiously, but it looks strained.
“I’m Amy.”
“Pazilya.”
“I know.”
She hesitates, shifting from one foot to the other.
“I heard what happened to your sister. I’m really sorry.”
My whole body tenses.
Great. The whole school is talking about me.
“What exactly did you hear?”
She blushes.
“Only that she was taken away. In China. And that she…”
She stops abruptly and bites her lip.
I say nothing.
What is there to say?
“It’s so horrible,” Amy says. Her words almost tumble over each other. “What’s happening there. I don’t understand how the world can just watch.”
She takes a deep breath.
“Sorry. I talk too much. My mom always says I should think before I speak, but…”
She trails off, shaking her head at herself.
I study her.
Most people barely know who we Uyghurs are. And here is a girl I don’t know who clearly has no idea what to say, but tries anyway.
“My parents fled from the Congo,” Amy says quietly. “From the war. But we have problems here too. Last month, my brother got beaten up by three guys. At the subway station.”
She gives a short laugh, but it sounds wrong.
“Broken nose. He jokes about it, says he looks like a boxer now. But at night, I sometimes hear him crying.”
“I’m sorry,” I say.
She shrugs.
“My parents keep saying that history repeats itself, but nobody wants to see it.”
For the first time in months, I feel something like connection.
“I’m in this group.”
Amy fiddles nervously with the straps of her backpack.
“Against right-wing extremism. We organize demos and stuff. There’s another one on Saturday, on the market square.”
She hesitates.
“Honestly, most of the time it feels pointless. We stand there with our signs, then everyone goes home and it’s as if nothing happened. But I don’t know what else to do.”
I nod. I don’t know what to say.
“Last time there were counter-protesters. Some guys yelled at us.”
She laughs again. It sounds strange, fake.
“My friends don’t want to come anymore. They think it’s too dangerous. I can’t even blame them.”
She looks at me and smiles tiredly.
I think of my sister. Of the people still being held in camps and prisons. Of Amy’s brother, crying at night. Of the two of us. Of my mother.
The pain in my chest returns, brief and throbbing.
Without thinking, I reach behind my ear and feel the bent clip of the hairpin. It presses uncomfortably into my skin.
“We could meet up sometime.”
Amy’s voice goes quiet.
“On Sunday? We could maybe go to a café, if you want.”
My first impulse is to run.
But I hear myself say, “Maybe.”
Amy blinks in surprise.
“Seriously?”
“I don’t know.” My heart is pounding. “I haven’t met up with anyone in a long time.”
“Then maybe you won’t come.”
Amy scribbles her number on a crumpled receipt. Her handwriting is barely legible, shaky.
“I’ll wait anyway. In case you make it after all.”
She presses the slip of paper into my hand. Her palm is sweaty.
“So, maybe see you Sunday.”
I only nod. I can’t say anything else.
Amy is already walking away. She turns around once more and raises her hand tentatively.
Then she is gone.
I take a deep breath and walk on to school. The paper is crumpled in my fist. When I enter the classroom, I put it in my pocket.
First period is math.
I haven’t done the homework.
Outside, it starts to drizzle. Single drops run down the windowpane. I see my reflection in it.
The hair clip is barely visible in the dim light.
It holds.
But for how long, I don’t know.

This story is fiction. All characters are invented. The background is based on documented reports, including the 2022 assessment of the situation in Xinjiang by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.
fields.author: Sophia Kanesarasa

fields.title: Die Weitergabe von Mutter zu Tochter: Das Körperbild
fields.description:
Die Weitergabe von Mutter zu Tochter: Das Körperbild
Eine persönliche Erfahrung
Eine Erinnerung, die fest in meinem Kopf verankert ist, ist die, wie meine Mutter im Badezimmer auf die Waage steigt und seufzt. Manchmal sagt sie etwas Negatives wie: „Ich habe schon wieder über die Ferien zugenommen!“ Oder sie betrachtet ihren Bauch im Spiegel.
Gewicht war schon immer ein Thema in unserem Haushalt. Dabei ernährt sich meine Mutter ausgewogen und bewegt sich regelmäßig. Trotzdem kann sie die kleinen Fettrollen an ihrem Bauch nicht einfach annehmen. Es wirkt manchmal, als würde ihr Blick genau dort hängen bleiben. Sie tut viel, um sie loszuwerden, unter anderem durch regelmäßigen Sport. Doch es scheint nie genug zu sein.
Jedes Mal, wenn sie auf die Waage steigt oder wir uns über unser Körperbild unterhalten, tut es mir ein kleines bisschen mehr weh. Dabei tut sie das vor allem für sich selbst. Meinem Vater ist ihr Gewicht egal, ihren Freunden ebenfalls und Fremden erst recht. Mein Vater selbst hat einen Bierbauch und trotzdem liebt sie ihn und hat ihn an ihrer Seite.
Als Kind habe ich nicht verstanden, was meine Mutter da macht. Ich habe angefangen, ihr Verhalten zu kopieren, so wie Kinder von ihren Eltern lernen. Ich stellte mich auf die Waage und betrachtete die lustige Zahl, die darauf erschien.
Doch als ich in die Pubertät kam, erwischte ich mich irgendwann dabei, wie ich in den Spiegel schaute und meinen Bauch betrachtete, genau wie meine Mutter es tat. Ich begann, über mein eigenes Gewicht nachzudenken. „Bin ich zu schwer?“
Seitdem fühlte sich die Waage manchmal wie eine Droge an. Ich stellte mich täglich darauf und ließ mir von der Zahl, die dort erschien, meine Stimmung vorgeben. Eine einzige Zahl konnte plötzlich bestimmen, wie ich mich an diesem Tag fühlte.
Dabei lag ich eigentlich immer eher an der Grenze zum Untergewicht als zum Übergewicht. Trotzdem schämte ich mich, besonders wenn wir in der Schule Sport hatten. Ich begann, mich mit anderen zu vergleichen. Oversized-Klamotten halfen mir dabei, mich und meine Scham zu verstecken.
Mittlerweile schaffe ich es immer öfter, die Waage einfach zur Seite zu stellen und mich nicht von einer Zahl bestimmen zu lassen. Trotzdem gibt es Tage, an denen ich mich „zu schwer“ fühle.
Versteht mich nicht falsch: Ein gesundes Verhältnis zu Ernährung und Bewegung ist wichtig. Auch der Wunsch, Gewicht zu verlieren, kann für manche Menschen ein persönliches und gesundheitliches Ziel sein. Problematisch wird es für mich dort, wo unser Körper und sein Gewicht bestimmen, wie wir über uns selbst denken und welchen Wert wir uns geben.
Denn viele Faktoren, die unser Gewicht beeinflussen, können wir gar nicht selbst bestimmen. Genetik spielt eine Rolle, ebenso wie Krankheiten und andere körperliche oder persönliche Umstände. Unser Körper ist nicht einfach etwas, das wir nach unseren Vorstellungen formen können.
Deshalb möchte ich euch etwas mitgeben: Sagt eurer Mutter, dass sie schön ist, so wie sie ist. Sagt euch selbst, dass ihr gut seid, so wie ihr seid. Und achtet darauf, was ihr vor euren eigenen Kindern eines Tages über euren Körper, euer Gewicht und das Aussehen anderer sagt.
Denn Kinder beobachten uns. Sie lernen von uns, wie sie die Welt und auch sich selbst betrachten sollen.
Passt auf euch auf. Seid freundlich zu euch selbst. Und seid stolz auf euch, so wie ihr seid und so, wie ihr lebt.
Vielen Dank fürs Lesen.
By Selina
